title: The Machine Will Not Go of Itself
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/anton-barba-kay
text:
All they want to do is to prevent us from doing. On our side, we want to prevent them from preventing us. That’s about as clearly as we all see it…it’s a beautiful, lucid, inspiring program.
—Henry James, The Tragic Muse

To celebrate the birthday of a nation is to believe that it is alive, as only creatures natal are. And to believe that it is alive is to believe that its umbilical origin deserves our regard and that it should be given to a future still to be accomplished—that a nation once founded can still be found again. We borrow this conviction, that the foundation of a state carries its meaning, from the Romans, who were the first to tell time from their city’s institution. But while the foundation of Rome was a yarn about lupine lactation, the American foundation was born from modern prose declared to all. In the written word was our beginning. And whereas Roman politics was fundamentally backward-looking, American politics has always regarded itself as coeval with beginning and unabashedly questing for its better days. The conviction that all could be otherwise—more perfect into union—is our national vocation. No other nation has ever rivaled the moral beauty of this promise.

It is shabby but entirely predictable that birthday two hundred fifty should have become one more flash point within the spicy slop of rancor and graft that swamps national life. If the effect of translating political life into the logic of social media has been to make the political personal and the personal political, it stands to reason that it should be difficult to inspirit the body politic with a common sense of patriotism beyond the scuffles for attention about the makeover of the Reflecting Pool, the differences between Freedom 250 and America250, and various cunning introductions of the cipher 1776. Fellow Americans, you may find that your spirits slump or jubilate. But I think we can all agree that the single greatest threat to the American project today is “the enemy within” or “the enemy of the Constitution,” as the president put it in his Fourth of July remarks. Here, at least, we stand on common ground.

Partisanship is not the problem; the problem is whether there is anything else left for us to go by. Conflicts over the most basic matters—peaceful transfer of power, legitimate speech, settled facts, the patent sense of the Constitution’s text—make it hard to cling to the hope that we may expect two hundred fifty years more of this. The fusion of politics with the attention economy, in particular, means that novelty is a winning incentive; and novelty is revolutionary, in the sense of selecting for the violation of norms and the dramatic interest of instability. As a matter of course, it renders the unthinkable thinkable and the atypical typical. Nor does it require great acumen to think that the United States finds itself teetering on a tenuous edge that is only a rage-post or three away from a transformation into a different regime.

A Popular Automatism

Yet these anxious uncertainties also exist alongside what is perhaps the deepest note underlying our common experience, which is one of automatism. Our politics by majuscule are themselves an answer to our hunger that something (anything) decisive happen. They express an inability to envision the longer continuity of what have come to feel like the elements of our social somnambulism: that Congress will remain jammed, that state services will deteriorate, that springs of political generosity will still wear out, that inequality of all sorts will become more grotesque, that social mobility will dry up, that young people will find it harder to lead decent and whole lives, that common reality will be eaten up in forms of private self-indulgence, that all kinds of human capacities will continue to be indiscriminately translated into their technological succedanea, that institutions of all kinds will sag into discredit, that all conflicts, elections, and discussions should be translated back into the master opposition of red and blue. You know this. I know this. The doomscroll, the bot-chat, the viral trigger: It goes on all the same. There are exceptions to the rigor of these tendencies. But on the whole, our sense of instability stems from the sense that nothing is uncertain (except everything).

This automatism bespeaks a withering of living options—the closing of the spiritual frontier, the sense that institutions no longer form people well, that public service is an ideal neither public nor in service. The two genuinely vital forces in American life right now are a vehement partisan enmity and the development of world-beating digital products and capacities: a furor of spontaneity over and against informational models so powerful that they threaten to obviate the need for human input of any sort. Both are destructive to the possibility of a common or political life as such.

The irony about this dead predictability is that the Constitution of the United States really does aim for the construction of a sort of glorious machine, one governed, as Madison wrote in “Federalist No. 43,” by “the transcendent law of nature and of nature’s God” as formulated by early-modern political science. Just as polarization is a term we have borrowed from the science of optics, many of the operative metaphors in the writing of Paine, Jefferson, Dickinson, Madison, Hamilton, and other Founders—those figures of speech in terms of which the project of a constitutional republic was formulated—were borrowed from celestial mechanics, as is the idea of “revolution,” of “checks and balances,” and of the states as stars spangling the flag. The doctrine of the separation of powers is centered on the cosmological view that all bodies stay in their right orbits by “those attractions and repulsions by which the balance of nature is preserved,” because if all were pulled by one force “they would introduce anarchy wherever they should go” (John Adams).11xJohn Adams, A Defence of the Constitutions of Government of the United States of America, letter XXV (London, 1788), 85–86. It is the same poetry of antagonism that checks the branches of government and that keeps the heavenly bodies in regular order.

If the idea of Newtonian government has long lost its shine in favor of vitalist metaphors—“government is not a machine, but a living thing,” as Woodrow Wilson put it22xWoodrow Wilson, The New Freedom: A Call for the Emancipation of the Generous Energies of a People, ed. W.B. Hale (New York, NY: Doubleday, Page & Company, 1913), 47.—it is either because we no longer regard normative politics as a science at all or because machines have come to seem to us like oppressive, inhuman objects. The notion that states should be regarded as properly organic (rather than mechanical) units has its roots in Counter-Enlightenment and Romantic thinkers, who had become disenchanted with liberal, contractual theories of the state. In Friedrich Schiller’s version, to name one: The organic form of ancient politics has given way in modernity to “an ingenious clock-work…a mechanical kind of collective life,”33xFriedrich Schiller, On the Aesthetic Education of Man, trans. Elizabeth M. Wilkinson and L.A. Willoughby (Oxford, England: Clarendon Press, 1968), 35. deadening in its effects. The idea of an organic society became a staple of right and left politics since the Progressive era, with its Spencerian influences, but it still subtends such notions as “rootless cosmopolitanism,” “organic society,” and “living Constitution.”

A Wrench in the Works

The idea of the Constitution nonetheless belongs to its Enlightenment situation, and, amid our habitual machine-bashing, it is easy to miss the fact that the machine had a divine status for many seventeenth- and eighteenth-century thinkers. That the universe as a whole was the Creator’s machine was a stock element of deism and natural theology: the view that there is one supreme God who has made the universe and then set it ticking according to the laws of nature. And, while deism and other forms of rational theology became less compelling as the iron cage of the sciences closed in, it is nonetheless true that the Founding Fathers’ faith was something more than their own cranky creed, since it meant that the government of the United States was an artifice of a larger, transcendent reality. The machine of government received its meaning on analogy with the machine of Creation as a whole. However heretical or transitory as a configuration of Christianity, it was Enlightenment deism that allowed the Constitution to instance, represent, and mediate a figure of a larger will and purpose. The Constitution itself is a machine raised to a higher power.

I say this because this divine figure was, for a time, a satisfactory solution to the modern problem of fitting the spirit of a people—the idea of a popular will and sovereignty—together with the prescribed and codified motions of government. Whether regarded as a noble lie of educated elites, or as an earnest compromise that would defang sectarian violence, or as a way of harnessing religious fervor to the national project itself, the deist idea in its peculiarly American version—with the disestablishment of a state church and with its friendly attitude toward industry, research, and commerce—has been the center of the nation’s dynamism toward all frontiers. For good or ill, it has been essential to the possibility of having a nation at all. And it is now being torn apart in two directions.

One direction has been toward legalism, technocracy, and regulatory drift. Carl Schmitt, the brilliant scholar who became Hitler’s jurist, stated his version of this point earlier in the twentieth century: “The sovereign, who in the deistic view of the world…had remained the engineer of the great machine, has been radically pushed aside. The machine now runs by itself.”44xCarl Schmitt, Political Theology, trans. George Schwab (Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Press, 2006), 48. The other direction has been toward avowals of a raw and spontaneous national self-assertion—whether in the form of a charismatic executive, “taking back control” (as champions of Brexit promised), closing borders, Tea Party austerity, or other strains of what is glossed as “populism.” Whereas the idea of popular sovereignty was once conjugated with that of the quasi-mechanical processes of government in and through the figure of the divine machine, they are now cast asunder in these two pathological forms: the evocation of an immediate popular will over and against the view that regulations, norms, treaties, and procedures should do most of the work of governing.

We have run through enough iterations of this conflict to see that these two tendences are now at open odds. The strength of the executive is currently expressed through the smashing of the legal and bureaucratic machine; while the institutional and bureaucratic apparatus, on the other hand, can do nothing but try to ensure that such an executive is ruled out in advance. Ghost and machine have come apart.

The Failure of Political Imagination

By sketching the conflict at maximum altitude, my point is not to reassure you that there is something to be said for both sides but to observe that the United States faces cracks in its foundation that won’t be remedied either by institutional tinkering or by high-minded pleas. Such alternatives themselves only reiterate the problem that our political imagination is failing us. This wide failure makes patent our inability to replace the figure of the divine machine—the metaphysics of liberalism that once facilitated shared political commitments.

The failure takes three concrete forms for us. The first is the degradation of the principle of mediation and heterogeneity noted in the Adams quotation above: the principle that the democratic will of the people is expressed primarily through fundamentally different institutions rather than through polls, media cycles, or even elections. The discrediting of the Electoral College, of an impartial judiciary, and of federal agencies, as well as of the independence of the legislative branch, all point back to the problem of celestial mechanics that Constitutional machinery was meant to solve: how to keep independent institutions in regular motion around a single center without either flying off from or surrendering to it. If Donald Trump has hardly been the first imperial president or the first disintermediating force in American politics—a tendency dating back to the adoption of the Seventeenth Amendment, if not the Civil War—he has obviously understood how to embody it. He does so through the monopoly he has come to wield over the Republican Party, as well as in his immediate mode of communicating, responding, and issuing policy in real time. Whether it is Trump or another, the executive has acquired a gravity that threatens to collapse all other bodies into itself. At the limit, such a collapse could mean the discrediting of the role of the electorate itself, since there is no intrinsic reason why we should always know to choose what is in our best interest. Populism need not be democratic.

The second is that, with the breakdown of the divine machine, the empirical sciences and traditional religion have fallen asunder as sources of legitimacy. The present Democratic left is reflexively technocratic and policy-oriented; it lacks a unifying moral vocabulary and grammar. Its pursuit of equality is formulated, justified, and pursued in terms of measurable outcomes, which are themselves rendered actionable through state processes. The figure in the second Trump administration most reviled by the left is therefore Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He threatens the presumption that public health should be above politics—on the heels of a pandemic crisis in which public health became politics itself. As the lawn sign puts it: “We believe in science.”

The MAGA right has, in turn, been by design rebuilt on a falsehood about the 2020 election (as if to express that facts themselves can hold no ultimate dominion over it). It has identified federal agencies and bureaucracies—the deep state—as one of its chief targets, because these institutions are ones whose mandate stems from expertise and technocratic continuity. And it has doubled down, accordingly, on a narrowing vision of the United States as a Christian nation ruled by the naked will of the (true) people—a will that finds itself broadcast live within the president’s own authenticity and in his concomitant assurances that we are living through something really pretty major here.

This conflict between parties dramatizes a characteristic fault line within modernity itself, between scientific truth and moral meaning; it has come to stand for the tensions between equality and freedom as such, which is why the United States remains world-historically interesting even in its current form. But no liberal democracy can carry on with scientific authority eccentric to some sense, however partial and illusory, of popular self-determination.

The third is the loss of a clear definition of what government is (or is not) for, in relation to other private or transcendent purposes. The deist constitutional machine was designed to operate independently from the more or less autonomous ends of the individuals populating it. Whether this was really or completely true, the idea of such a machine was nonetheless to create the framework within which a variety of pursuits and creeds could be conjugated into one state. This is what is supposed to make America a divine model for all peoples rather than just another nation alongside them. And, while machines seem dead to us because they are not motivated by internal purpose, this same scission of machine from purpose is another formulation for the division of private from public that has long been breaking down—in part under pressure from our unstable understandings of “freedom” and “equality,” which, in the presence of new technological capacities for measurement and standardization, have invited legislative creep into private life.

This breakdown, in turn, means that the control of the government has acquired a newly transcendent inflection. It doesn’t need saying that both left and right have in their ways continuously blurred the lines between the transcendent and political. The current White House enjoys and encourages a quasi-transcendent devotion among many of its followers, just as peak woke of the 2010s has often been compared to a puritanical movement with claims to a supra-political justice. The vicissitudes of this relationship between politics and religion is at the center of Isaiah Berlin’s well-known “Two Concepts of Liberty,” in which he contrasts a liberal state that secures a merely procedural or “negative” liberty and one that, in working to implement some positive vision of the good life, is coercive, intrusive, and expansive in actual practice. As the Founding machine was intended as the medium of a liberal pluralism, the organic community that is now vying for its place necessarily continues to present us with the spectacle of two political religions at holy war with each other.

A Literate Republic, If You Can Keep It

The United States is getting old—not in years but in our imagination of a form of government that has drifted too far from practice. The figure of the divine machine was the product of another religious and technological situation; we cannot simply will it otherwise. Yet the metaphysical machinery of liberalism once sanctioned its regular order by harmonizing the three conflicts I have sketched—establishing independent foci of mediation, harmonizing scientific reason with religious purpose, and distinguishing public life from private. And these distinctions will still collapse toward one authoritarian center, so long as our actual uses of media and technology are misaligned with the artifice of government. Because the machine of government has never been made of material springs, coils, and balances; it is, instead, mainly a thing of words.

To underline the single most significant misalignment between republican theory and technological practice: For much of American history, the voice of the Constitutional machine was the printing press. The practices, habits, attitudes, and institutions of literacy embedded and affirmed the norms tempering the conflicts I have noted. Not only do social media and digital news erode the quality of public speech, they also undermine the very idea that there is something like a unified “public” we should serve. Printed media create a common sense of readership; they give voice to groups of people who did not previously understand themselves to exist as such. Digital media, by contrast, incentivize existing social groups to classify and emphasize ever newer points of difference among ourselves. It is no longer authors who write their audience into unity; it is immediate audience feedback that creates content in the image of its own preferences. Whereas printed media, in aiming to persuade a public into being, encourages an ideal rhetorical center, digital media wins followers through ranting oppositions. And while printed media created a shared presumption to impartiality, digital media take things personally. As printed media formed publics, digital media now deform them.

The Constitutional machine was thus able to project itself as an ideal of balance, measure, equilibrium, and proportion in and through the printing press. The Constitution was itself a compromise between the nation’s original sin and its better promise; it was formulated as a resolution to the problem of mediating forces at political odds. But the printing press was the medium by which we internalized this quasi-mechanical framework into a national ethic and creed. It served to communicate the transcendent meaning of politics with the technological apparatus of our ordinary imagination. In allowing us to extend our private self-interest into our political institutions, it was the technology of the US government itself: the machine whereby apple pie was turned into stars and stripes.

We therefore have a sort of choice to make about our way forward. We could choose to recommit to being what we have been: a literate nation, a “nation of lawyers” bound by and mediated by the letter of the law that governs us. We cannot turn back the clock, but we can slow it down to work out new compromises—such as existed in the twentieth century, when printed literacy started to yield its informational monopoly to radio and TV. This would mean acknowledging the close connections between reading, writing, thinking, persuasion, and democratic government itself. It would mean forming young people who can read better than they scroll. It would mean accepting the presence of some institutional gatekeepers that were once immensely powerful, even if now barely credible. It would also mean moderating or curtailing some of our national uses of social media. Unlimited speech, social media, and the United States: In the long run, we can keep only two of those three.

Or we could refigure government into digital terms. We could choose to consecrate algorithmic authority as a new mediation of sovereign will and automatic process: a new kind of sovereign integrating the part with the whole in a granular and seamless way. This option would allow each user to “engage” with government decisions in infinitely patient and bespoke terms. It would allow us to streamline many tedious, inefficient, and irrational aspects of government (like paying taxes, filing lawsuits, or reading legislative bills). It could, on aggregate, allow for a fairer distribution of resources and outcomes (reducing, say, the influence of wealth on litigation). And its all-seeing eye could of course keep us safer.

This digital option may no longer require voting, debate, or persuasion. Or we could still do those things for the sake of appearances, telling ourselves that elected officials are still in charge even as most kinds of state capacity and decisions are in fact being outsourced to AI—and even as large language models become our figure of superhuman, “unbiased” judgment. I am not suggesting the United States will or can or should pull it off, but it is clear that for any nation-state to remain vibrant and viable, it will have to find a way of consciously reenvisioning the work of government in relation to the digital sphere: whether as its antagonist or as its very own self. Because, pushed to its limits, AI already promises to be the medium of an ultimate organic sovereign, sublimating a quasi-personal “spontaneity” and quasi-objective “certainty” into one master device taking all into account.

The machinery of liberalism was designed to render extraordinary and unforeseen acts of individual political judgment—political miracles—irrelevant, if not impossible. This is what it once meant to have a government of “laws, not of men”: that the people themselves are mediated by a systematic form rather than counting on the lucky presence of a genius or a good monarch. This self-conception has been only half true, since without periodic achievements of American political heroism—a heroism that has, at times, understood how to balance conviction against pragmatism—the republic would not be here today. It is in such balance that we have found the measures of our justice. But as the machine threatens to run into the ground on auto, only the rediscovery of an ideal poise of forces can arrest our collapse toward a single and immediate center. Only such a miracle can save us.
